messages.author: e5fcf5da4d09ceca
messages.subject: [distance-sampling] %CV on estimated density and abundance
parts:
Hello everyone,
I'm a beginner with distance sampling software though i found it very user friendly and managed to cope with it at some extent. However i have some question to make regarding % coefficient of variation on the estimated density and abundance particularly at "Global level of resolution of estimates" 
I have two transect with two species observed from my study site i.e. cattle and puku antelope. Cattle was observed only in one of the transect while puku got observed in all the two transect. So i first estimated density and abundance transect wise to see the estimates using MCDS with habitat categories (factor with four levels) as covariate. With this i got the estimate which i can say "low % CV of density and abundance estimates" presumably the estimates are okay.

I estimated first density of each species per transect i.e. cattle had 34.33%CV on the density and abundance each while puku had 24.195 and 13.11% as CV on transect one and two on density and abundance estimate respectively.

Then, I estimated density and abundance of these two species for the entire study areas in order to deduce an overall density and abundance of them. For cattle's estimates i got  36.34% as a %CV on density and abundance each while puku had  64.62% as %CV on density and abundance each. It can be observed that there's large increase on the  %CV on the estimated parameters (density and abundance) particularly for puku.

My question is, what makes such an  increase in %CV observed when i'm trying to estimate i term it as  an "overall" density and abundance particularly for puku antelope? And is there any way/means to/at least improve the estimates as i guess the large %CV of the estimates will be associated with large standard error thus posing a difficult  moments in deducing the final results particularly ones for puku estimates.

Kind regards
Koggani

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] %CV on estimated density and abundance
parts:
Koggani

Your interpretation of analysis and questions about precision indicate you are paying close attention to your findings.

However, rather than discuss the details of your CV comparisons, I'll comment upon your study design.  Your data file and your description indicate your study has only two transects.  With only two transects, it is difficult to make inferences about your entire study area.  It is better to have more short transects scattered throughout the area of interest to make more reliable estimates not only of density or abundance, but also of the precision of those estimates.

Overall uncertainty in estimates of density across a study area stem from two sources: a) uncertainty in the estimates of the detection function parameters and b) variability in encounter rate between transects.  The second of these sources is ignored when density estimates are computed at the transect level; as you did with your first analysis.  The second assessment (for the entire study area) has larger CVs because the between-transect variability in encounter rate is included.

The most common scenario for performing animal surveys is to estimate density or abundance for a study area that is sampled (when using distance sampling) by a number of transects.   Variability in encounters between transects tells a great deal about how variable animal density is across the study area.     (If all transects have the same encounter rate, we conclude animal density is homogeneous.)  You can see that understanding this variability in encounter rates between transects is not possible with only a single transect, and still quite challenging with only two transects.

The answer to your final question about how to improve estimates in your study area is to revisit your survey design replacing few long transects with several short transects.  Perhaps visit our online training materials, concentrating on estimation of precision:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter2/#measures-of-precision
